questions.stem: What is the purpose of a titration?

options.text: To measure the temperature of a reaction
To find the exact volume of one solution needed to react completely with another
To measure the mass of a solid

questions.explanation: A titration is used to find the exact volume of one solution (e.g., acid) needed to react completely with a known volume of another solution (e.g., alkali), and can be used to calculate unknown concentrations.

questions.stem: In a titration, which piece of equipment is used to add the acid gradually?
questions.explanation: A burette is used to add the acid (or alkali) gradually and precisely. It has a tap that allows controlled addition, drop by drop near the end point.

questions.stem: What is the 'end point' of a titration?

options.text: When the indicator changes colour permanently, showing the reaction is complete

questions.explanation: The end point is when the indicator permanently changes colour, indicating that the acid and alkali have completely reacted (neutralisation is complete).

questions.stem: Why is a conical flask used to hold the alkali rather than a beaker?

options.text: Its shape allows easy swirling to mix the solutions without spillage
It is easier to read the volume

questions.explanation: A conical flask has a narrow neck that prevents splashing when the flask is swirled to mix the acid and alkali during the titration.

questions.stem: Why is a rough (trial) titration carried out first?

options.text: To get an approximate value for the end point, so subsequent titrations can be done more accurately
To check the indicator is working

questions.explanation: A rough titration gives an approximate volume. In subsequent titrations, the acid can be added quickly up to near this volume, then added drop by drop to get an accurate end point.

questions.stem: What should you do with the titration results to get the most accurate answer?

options.text: Calculate the mean of concordant results (results within 0.10 cm³ of each other)

questions.explanation: Concordant results (those that are very close together, typically within 0.10 cm³) are averaged to give the most accurate titre value. Anomalous results are excluded.

questions.stem: A pipette is used in titrations to measure:

options.text: An exact, fixed volume of the alkali

questions.explanation: A pipette is used to measure an exact, fixed volume (usually 25.0 cm³) of the alkali and transfer it into the conical flask. This ensures precision.
